extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of philosophy (metaphysics, ethics), scholars of Schopenhauer
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition from Schopenhauer's metaphysical-ethical treatise on the nature of the will, human suffering, egoism, wrong, and property; presents normative/diagnostic claims about life and moral phenomena. Useful for understanding criteria Schopenhauer uses to evaluate human action, institutions, and psychological states.

rubrics_metrics.name: Life is essentially suffering / incapable of true blessedness
rubrics_metrics.description: In its whole plan life is capable of no true blessedness, but is in its very nature suffering in various forms, and throughout a state of misery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Schopenhauer argues a priori that the human world is the kingdom of chance and error; empirical confirmation is everywhere (hospitals, prisons, battlefields, Dante's hell). He uses examples (Hopelessness in hospitals, Ugolino, etc.) to make the conviction vivid. This claim underpins subsequent moral and metaphysical conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Life is tragedy in the large, comedy in the detail
rubrics_metrics.description: Surveyed as a whole life is always a tragedy; gone through in detail it has the character of a comedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The daily petty mishaps, momentary irritations, and chance-driven events make life comic in its particulars, while the long-term frustrated aims, unfulfilled wishes, and death give life's broad character a tragic form. Schopenhauer uses this duality to explain how people can both laugh at small misfortunes and yet live under tragic conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ennui and the creation of imaginary worlds (superstition) as coping/occupation
rubrics_metrics.description: When the spirit is not satisfied by ordinary cares and occupations, it creates an imaginary world in the form of superstitions and spends time and strength on it; such imaginary converse often becomes more interesting than real human intercourse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This phenomenon is especially marked in societies with easy material life (e.g., Hindus, Greeks, Romans, later Italians/Spaniards). Schopenhauer treats superstition as both a symptom of human need (for help/support and diversion) and as having a non-contemptible gain (occupational/diversionary value), while also noting its dangers (wasting time at moments when practical action is needed).

rubrics_metrics.name: Assertion of the will (fundamental mode of action)
rubrics_metrics.description: The assertion of the will is continuous willing itself, undisturbed by any knowledge, expressing chiefly the satisfaction of bodily wants and the maintenance of the individual and propagation of the species.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Schopenhauer describes the assertion of the will as the body-objectification of the will: motives are the manner in which will appears. The important point is that something is willed and the intensity of that willing. Most people live with knowledge always serving the aims of the will (know what they wish and act to attain it).

rubrics_metrics.name: Denial of the will (voluntary renunciation as moral/soteriological act)
rubrics_metrics.description: Voluntary renunciation of satisfaction (especially of sexual impulse) based on no motive but on knowledge is a denial or suppression of the will to live—an act of self-suppression that leads toward salvation/conquest of the world.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such denial is hard and painful self-conquest because it contradicts the body's objectification of the will. Schopenhauer treats renunciation as the only avenue to suppress willing and attain freedom; he warns it is exceptional and difficult for most men.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sexual impulse as the decisive and strongest assertion of the will to live
rubrics_metrics.description: The sexual impulse expresses the most decided assertion of the will to live, going beyond mere self-maintenance because it asserts life beyond the individual and seeks propagation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Schopenhauer points to biological facts and mythic symbolism (phallus, lingam, Proserpine/pomegranate) to illustrate how generation is the vehicle by which the will perpetuates itself and thereby reasserts suffering and death. The genitals are described as the focus of will, opposite the brain (representative of knowledge).

rubrics_metrics.name: Generation perpetuates suffering and death (biological justification of shame and original sin symbolism)
rubrics_metrics.description: By producing new individuals generation reasserts suffering and death in the world; the begotten inherits the phenomenon of will and its accompanying misery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Schopenhauer links this to theological/mythical motifs (Adam's transgression, Proserpine) to explain shame connected with generation and why religious traditions portray procreation as implicated in original guilt and suffering.

rubrics_metrics.name: Egoism arises from the principium individuationis (time and space)
rubrics_metrics.description: Time and space (principium individuationis) make multiplicity possible; because each knowing individual appears to itself as the whole will, it places its own existence and well-being before all else—this stance is egoism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The individual experiences others only as ideas and thus prioritizes its own preservation, which explains readiness to sacrifice others for one's own continuation. This metaphysical grounding explains moral psychology (self-centeredness) and is presented as the source of interpersonal conflict.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflict of individuals (Eris / bellum omnium contra omnes) as an unavoidable source of suffering
rubrics_metrics.description: The inner contradiction of the will to live, manifesting in multiplicity of individuals, produces an unquenchable source of suffering through perpetual conflict among individuals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrations include wild-beast fights, mobs freed from law, tyrants, wars—conflict appears both in tragic and absurd (comic) forms. Schopenhauer treats social/political violence as natural consequences of egoism rooted in individuation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wrong defined as transgression into another's sphere of assertion of will
rubrics_metrics.description: Wrong (injustice) is when one individual breaks through the limits of the assertion of another's will—either by destroying/injuring another body, forcing its powers to serve one's own will, or seizing goods produced by another's labor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Schopenhauer analyses wrong abstractly and concretely: cannibalism and murder are its clearest types; mutilation or injury is of the same nature differing only in degree; slavery and wrongful seizure of property are also forms of wrong because they appropriate another's bodily powers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Property right grounded in labour (work theory of property)
rubrics_metrics.description: True (moral) right of property is based solely on work: property belongs to the person who produced, cultivated, improved, or preserved it by his own powers, not to mere past enjoyment or simple occupation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Schopenhauer rejects first-occupation theories (e.g., Kant's claim) and the idea that mere avowal of exclusion grants moral right. He uses examples (cultivated field, first hunter) and Manu law to support labour-based property rights, and argues that mere preoccupation without improvement gives no moral claim to exclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remorse (pang of conscience) arises from recognition of opposing the same will
rubrics_metrics.description: When one does wrong (e.g., murder) a distinct feeling of remorse arises because the wrong-doer recognizes obscurely that he is the same will as the victim and thus rends himself by acting against the will.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Schopenhauer treats remorse as an immediate feeling—not abstract knowledge—that wounds peace of mind. He promises further analysis later (conscience as manifestation of inner conflict) but here links remorse to the metaphysical unity of will.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral equivalence continuum: injury, mutilation, murder differ only by degree
rubrics_metrics.description: Mutilation, injury, or a mere blow are to be regarded as in their nature the same as murder, differing only in degree.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This supports the earlier definition of wrong and emphasizes the seriousness of acts that degrade, harm, or appropriate another's bodily powers even when falling short of killing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vanity / opinion_of_others as empty show masking inner misery
rubrics_metrics.description: People often display pomp and splendour to seem fortunate in others' eyes; the opinion of others is a chief aim of efforts though essentially empty (vanitas).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under the false show miseries accumulate unseen; external semblances conceal suffering. Schopenhauer uses the etymology of 'vanity' and social observations to critique striving for reputation as futile and deceptive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Death and generation as symmetric elements for the will (death does not trouble the will)
rubrics_metrics.description: Death does not trouble the will because it belongs to life itself; generation counterbalances death by ensuring the continuation of the will—thus those who fully assert life can await death without fear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Schopenhauer previously explained (in Fourth Book beginning) that awareness changes attitude to death: conscious assertion of life allows fearless facing of death, and in general the will encompasses both death and generation as parts of its ongoing assertion.
